tur25-0: Scoliosis: C and S Curves, Cobb Angle, Exercise, Bracing and Surgery | İhsan Eren
tur25-1: What scoliosis is, C and S curves, the Cobb angle and why the growth years matter; school bags, one-sided habits and joint flexibility; treatments past and present, and a comparison of exercise, bracing and surgery.
tur25-2: A sideways curve of the spine that also twists around its own axis. It most often appears in adolescence, in a form with no known cause (idiopathic), and it is usually painless. Because it can progress during rapid growth, spotting it early matters. In this guide we explain curve types, how curves are measured on X-rays, why growth matters and how treatment has changed over time, drawing on research and on clinical experience and keeping the two clearly apart.
tur25-14: Scoliosis is diagnosed when an X-ray shows the spine curving sideways by 10 degrees or more, with rotation of the vertebrae. So scoliosis is not just a sideways bend but a three-dimensional change in shape: as the vertebrae shift sideways they also rotate around their own axis, pushing the ribs backwards on one side. In about 80% of cases no specific cause is found; this is called idiopathic scoliosis. About 30% of adolescents diagnosed with it have a family member with scoliosis.
tur25-15: Small curves are about equally common in girls and boys, but larger, progressive curves are much more common in girls: according to the Scoliosis Research Society (SRS), girls are 5–8 times more likely than boys to have a curve progress far enough to need treatment.
tur25-16: How it differs from poor posture
tur25-17: Poor posture, muscle spasm due to pain or a difference in leg length can also make the spine look tilted to one side. In these functional curves the vertebrae are not rotated, and the curve disappears when the cause is removed, for example when standing up straight, bending forward or lying down. In true (structural) scoliosis, a hump appears on one side of the back when bending forward. According to the SRS, a difference in leg length does not cause scoliosis, but it can make a curve look more noticeable.
tur25-19: On an X-ray taken from behind, a spine with scoliosis often looks like the letter C or S. A C curve has a single arc. An S curve has two arcs facing opposite directions, one in the chest region and one in the lower back; one may be the main (structural) curve and the other a secondary curve that develops to balance the trunk, or both may be structural. Curves are named by where their apex lies: thoracic (chest), thoracolumbar (where the chest meets the lower back) and lumbar (lower back); curves in the chest region most often point to the right.
tur25-20: Straight spineSeen from behind, the vertebrae are stacked one above the other.
tur25-21: C curveA single arc; the shoulders and waist may become uneven.
tur25-22: S curveTwo arcs facing opposite ways, in the chest and lower back.
tur25-23: The drawings are simplified to show curve types; they are not real X-ray images.
tur25-24: When planning surgery, surgeons classify curves in more detail (for example with the Lenke classification); physiotherapists likewise choose scoliosis-specific exercises according to the curve type. So even two curves of the same size may need different programmes.
tur25-25: More detail: SRS patient handbook
tur25-26: The size of a scoliosis curve is measured with the Cobb angle on a standing X-ray of the whole spine. At each end of the curve, the vertebrae that tilt most towards each other (the end vertebrae) are chosen; the angle between lines drawn along the upper and lower surfaces of these vertebrae is the size of the curve. A curve of 10 degrees or more counts as scoliosis.
tur25-27: The measurement has a margin of error: different measurements of the same X-ray can differ by 5–10 degrees, and the angle can vary by about 5 degrees over the course of a day. So a change of a few degrees does not on its own mean progression; decisions are based on measurements over time together with the examination.
tur25-29: In children who are still growing, usually close monitoring; scoliosis-specific exercises can be a first step.
tur25-31: In children who are still growing, a brace is usually recommended; exercises continue alongside the brace.
tur25-33: In children who are still growing, surgery is considered. The threshold is lower for lumbar curves (35–40 degrees); curves beyond these limits tend to keep progressing into adulthood.
tur25-34: These limits are the general approach in the SRS patient handbook; the final decision is your doctor's.
tur25-35: Cobb angleGold: end vertebrae; green: the apex of the curve. The angle where the dashed lines meet is the size of the curve.
tur25-36: Checking at home and measuring remaining growth
tur25-37: Forward bend testIf one side of the back rises when bending forward, there is rotation. A scoliometer measures this difference in degrees.
tur25-38: Risser signThe growth cartilage along the rim of the pelvis turns to bone in stages 1 to 4 and fuses at stage 5. Stages 0–1 mean more growth remains.
tur25-39: In school screening, trunk rotation is measured with a scoliometer; in a study of 966 students in Portugal, 7 degrees or more was taken as marked rotation and was found in 4.2% of students. The Risser sign is read from the rim of the pelvis on an X-ray and is used to estimate how much growth remains.

tur25-42: The most common type (about 80%). By age at onset it is divided into infantile (under 3), juvenile (3–10) and adolescent (10 and over); the adolescent type is the most common.
tur25-44: Caused by vertebrae that formed incompletely or joined together before birth; usually noticed at an early age.
tur25-46: Can develop from muscle imbalance in conditions such as cerebral palsy or muscle diseases, or from tissue laxity in connective tissue disorders such as Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
tur25-48: A curve that began in adolescence and progresses slowly in adulthood, or scoliosis that appears later in life from wear of the discs and joints (degenerative).
tur25-49: Why do the growth years matter so much?
tur25-50: Curves progress most during the rapid growth spurt of adolescence. The peak of the growth spurt comes earlier in girls than in boys; in girls, the period before the first menstrual period is the riskiest. So in young people going through the growth spurt (roughly 10–18 years old) a curve can increase even over a few months.
tur25-52: In a classic study that followed untreated children with curves of 5–29 degrees until the end of growth, the curve progressed in 23%. Progression was best predicted by the size of the curve, age, the Risser sign and whether menstruation had started.
tur25-54: For curves of 20–29 degrees, the chance of progression was reported as 68% in children with most of their growth still ahead (Risser 0–1) and about 23% in those further along in growth (Risser 2–4).
tur25-56: In 120 girls treated with a brace, the curve progressed to 45 degrees or more in 83% of those whose curve exceeded 30 degrees at the peak of the growth spurt, compared with 4% of those at 30 degrees or less. In 90% of the children, growth stopped within 3.6 years of the peak.
tur25-57: After growth ends, curves under 30 degrees rarely progress. Larger curves can progress slowly in adulthood: in patients in Denmark followed for 41 years on average, curves increased by 0.2–0.5 degrees per year on average, but people differed widely. People whose curve exceeds 50 degrees at the end of growth have a higher risk of breathlessness later in life.
tur25-58: School bags, one-sided habits and joint flexibility
tur25-59: Families ask about this more than almost anything else. We set out what research shows and what we see in the clinic separately.
tur25-60: According to the SRS, heavy bags, poor posture and sport do not cause scoliosis or make a curve worse; however, a heavy bag can cause back pain.
tur25-61: Among 966 students aged 10–16 in Portugal, bag weight and posture habits were not associated with scoliosis, whereas poor sitting and standing habits were associated with low back pain. This was a cross-sectional study, so it cannot show cause and effect.
tur25-62: In one study, 51.4% of 70 children with idiopathic scoliosis had generalised joint laxity (hypermobility), compared with 19% of healthy peers; laxity was not related to the size of the curve. The authors recommend checking for joint laxity in these children when planning physiotherapy.
tur25-63: Among 100 girls doing rhythmic gymnastics, scoliosis was found in 12%, compared with 1.1% of their peers. The authors described the combination of joint laxity, delayed puberty and repeated one-sided loading of the growing spine as a “dangerous triad”. This too was an observational study.
tur25-64: What do we see in the clinic?
tur25-66: In young people going through the growth spurt, always carrying a bag on the same shoulder, constantly carrying a heavy object or a musical instrument on the same side, and habits that load one side can make postural asymmetry more pronounced. When connective tissue flexibility is also present, as in benign joint hypermobility syndrome, we see that these asymmetries and back pain can be more marked. This does not mean that one-sided loading causes structural scoliosis; but it is a good reason to spread the load across both sides during the growth years.
tur25-67: This is based on clinical experience, not on research findings; it may not apply to everyone.
tur25-68: Carry the bag on both shoulders using both straps; keep its weight under 10–15% of body weight, with heavy items close to the back.
tur25-69: If your child does a one-sided sport or activity, there is no need to stop; balancing exercises that also work the other side can be added.
tur25-70: In children with very flexible joints, strengthening and posture control come before stretching.
tur25-72: A short history of scoliosis treatment
tur25-73: Scoliosis treatment has come a long way, from stretching tables to computer-designed braces and operations that guide growth. Some methods were tried and abandoned; most of those in use today have been tested in randomised trials over the past 30 years.
tur25-75: Hippocrates used a table that worked by stretching and pressing on the spine.
tur25-76: The first spinal fusion operation was performed (initially in spinal tuberculosis).
tur25-77: Katharina Schroth, observing how her own scoliotic trunk changed with breathing, developed a three-dimensional exercise method based on breathing and posture.
tur25-78: The Milwaukee brace came into use.
tur25-79: The Risser cast and the Risser sign, which shows remaining growth, were described.
tur25-80: Harrington rods began the era of correction with metal implants.
tur25-81: The Boston brace, which reaches only to the armpits and is less visible, was developed.
tur25-83: Electrical stimulation of the muscles was tried; in a multicentre study presented in 1993, progression stopped in about 80% of girls wearing a brace, whereas in the electrical stimulation and observation-only groups the curve increased by 6 degrees or more over 5 years in about 70%. The method was abandoned.
tur25-84: Three-dimensional correction of the spine with the Cotrel-Dubousset system became widespread; in the 1990s, pedicle screws began to be used in the thoracic vertebrae.
tur25-85: BrAIST became the first large randomised trial to show that bracing reduces the need for surgery.
tur25-86: The international SOSORT guideline placed scoliosis-specific physiotherapy exercises and bracing at the core of treatment during growth.
tur25-87: In the USA, a vertebral body tethering device, which aims to correct the curve in growing children without fusing the spine, received humanitarian use approval.
tur25-88: The Cochrane review of exercise was updated; the CONTRAIS trial in Sweden showed that a night-time brace can reduce progression in moderate curves.
tur25-89: Treatment options: for whom, for what, and what does the evidence say?
tur25-90: According to the guideline of the International Society on Scoliosis Orthopaedic and Rehabilitation Treatment (SOSORT), the aim of treatment during growth is to prevent or limit progression of the curve. Treatment is planned according to the curve angle, the curve type, remaining growth, the appearance of the trunk and the person's preferences.
tur25-93: Small curves; curves that have stopped growing and are not progressing.
tur25-96: Check-ups should be frequent during the growth spurt.
tur25-98: Small and moderate curves; alongside the brace for those wearing one.
tur25-99: To limit progression and improve posture and the appearance of the trunk.
tur25-101: Low or very low certainty; some studies show benefit, others no difference from general exercise.
tur25-103: Young people with moderate curves who are still growing and do not want a full-time brace.
tur25-104: To stop progression with a brace worn only during sleep.
tur25-105: Success in the CONTRAIS trial was 76%, compared with 53% with physical activity alone.
tur25-107: Those who are still growing, with curves between 20–25 and 40–45 degrees.
tur25-108: To prevent the curve reaching the surgical threshold; it does not straighten the curve.
tur25-109: Success in BrAIST was 72%, compared with 48% with observation; over 90% in those wearing it 13 hours a day or more.
tur25-111: Progressive large curves; cases where bracing has not been enough.
tur25-112: To partly correct the curve and stabilise it by fusing the vertebrae.
tur25-113: The most common operation; correction is usually partial.
tur25-115: Selected young people who are still growing.
tur25-116: To correct the curve without fusion by guiding growth.
tur25-117: Of the 57 patients whose data supported approval, 43 avoided fusion at 2 years; problems such as tether breakage and overcorrection were reported.
tur25-119: These exercises rest on three core principles: three-dimensional self-correction of the trunk, holding the corrected posture steady, and carrying this posture into daily life (sitting, carrying a bag, studying). Education and, where needed, psychological support go alongside them. There are seven best-known schools worldwide: Lyon (France), Schroth (Germany), SEAS (Italy), Barcelona (BSPTS, Spain), Dobomed and FITS (Poland) and Side Shift (UK). In the Schroth method, breathing directed according to the direction of rotation is also part of the programme.
tur25-120: The evidence is mixed. In a study of 45 adolescents in Türkiye, Schroth exercises done in the clinic with a physiotherapist reduced the curve angle, spinal rotation and rib hump over 24 weeks, whereas findings worsened in the groups exercising alone at home or not exercising. In the 2024 Cochrane review of 13 studies and 583 adolescents, however, the certainty of the evidence was low or very low: compared with general exercise, scoliosis-specific exercises probably reduce trunk rotation, and when done together with a brace they may slightly reduce progression. In the CONTRAIS trial of 135 adolescents in Sweden, scoliosis-specific exercise was no better than physical activity alone for moderate curves (success 58% vs 53%).
tur25-121: Those who benefit most from exercise are young people who keep up the programme regularly and manage to carry the corrected posture into daily life. The benefit is seen not only in the angle but also in postural awareness, pain and the young person's confidence in their own body. When a curve needs a brace, exercise does not replace it.
tur25-122: A brace does not straighten the curve; it aims to stop it progressing until growth ends. Today mostly rigid braces that reach to the armpits (such as the Boston brace) and Chêneau-type braces that apply three-dimensional pressure against the curve are used; night-time braces worn only during sleep are another option. In the BrAIST trial of 383 adolescents in the USA and Canada, the success rate in preventing the curve from reaching 50 degrees, the surgical threshold, was 72% with a brace and 48% with observation alone. The effect depended on how long the brace was worn. In the CONTRAIS trial in Sweden, a night-time brace was more successful than physical activity alone at preventing progression of more than 6 degrees in moderate curves (76% vs 53%).
tur25-123: Surgery, trunk balance and large curves
tur25-124: Surgery is usually considered when non-surgical treatment has not been enough. The most common criteria are a curve of more than 45 degrees in young people who are still growing, more than 40–50 degrees in people who have finished growing, and progression. Pain that does not respond to non-surgical treatment, effects on lung function and appearance also play a part in the decision. The most common operation is fusion, in which the spine is corrected with screws and rods and the vertebrae are fused.
tur25-125: A large angle on its own does not mean surgery. In 117 untreated patients followed for about 50 years in the USA, back pain was more common than in their peers, but their ability to carry out daily activities did not differ and mortality was not increased; a curve of more than 50 degrees at the end of growth, however, raised the risk of breathlessness later in life. So the decision is made with a spinal surgeon, based on whether the curve is progressing, whether the trunk is balanced, pain, lung function and the person's expectations.
tur25-126: In some patients who have finished growing, whose trunk is balanced (the body has compensated for the curve), whose curve is not progressing and whose daily life is not restricted, we see surgeons not recommending or postponing surgery even when the angle is large. For these patients, regular check-ups and strengthening and posture exercises remain the focus. Loss of trunk balance, increasing pain or progression of the curve can change the decision.

tur25-128: Unbalanced trunkThe trunk has shifted to one side; the plumb line falls outside the centre of the pelvis.

tur25-130: Scoliosis exercises should be tailored to the individual. The location, direction, size and flexibility of the curve, remaining growth and pain differ in every young person; one-sided exercises (for example a side plank or stretch weighted to one side) may not work if they are not chosen for the curve type. So plan scoliosis-specific exercises with a physiotherapist trained in these methods, based on the examination and X-rays.
tur25-131: The exercises below, by contrast, are general exercises that work both sides of the body equally. As long as they do not cause pain, you can usually do them safely; they strengthen the trunk muscles and support posture, but they do not straighten the curve on their own and do not replace scoliosis-specific exercises. If pain increases, or you get numbness or tingling in your arms or legs, stop the exercise and ask your doctor.
tur25-132: The test on the first card is a simple check you can do at home during the growth years.
tur25-133: Lie on your side with your elbow under your shoulder and your knees bent. Lift your hips to make a straight line from your head to your knees, then lower slowly. Do both sides equally; if one side needs more work because of your curve, your physiotherapist will decide.
tur25-135: Two types are seen in adults: idiopathic scoliosis that began in adolescence and progresses slowly, and degenerative scoliosis that develops later in life from wear of the discs and small joints. According to the SRS, curves under 30 degrees carry a similar risk of back pain to having no scoliosis, whereas untreated curves over 50–60 degrees are more likely to cause low back pain.
tur25-136: More detail: Low back pain and Spinal stenosis guides
tur25-138: According to the SRS, children with scoliosis can do any sport as long as they have no back pain. The international guideline also recommends not giving up sport, even during brace treatment, because of its general health and psychological benefits; however, no sport replaces treatment on its own.
tur25-139: According to research, no: the Scoliosis Research Society (SRS) states that heavy bags, poor posture and sport do not cause scoliosis or make a curve worse, and a study of 966 students in Portugal also found no association between bag weight or posture habits and scoliosis. A heavy bag can, however, cause back pain. In our clinical experience, one-sided loading can make postural asymmetry and pain more pronounced in young people who are in the growth spurt and have flexible joints, so we recommend carrying the bag on both shoulders.
tur25-140: What is the difference between a C curve and an S curve?
tur25-141: A C curve has a single arc in the spine. An S curve has two arcs facing opposite directions, one in the chest region and one in the lower back. In both, the size of the curve is measured on X-ray with the Cobb angle; treatment decisions take the curve type, the angle and remaining growth into account together.
tur25-142: Can my child with scoliosis do sport?
tur25-143: Yes. According to the SRS, children with scoliosis can do any sport as long as they have no back pain; the international guideline (SOSORT) also recommends not giving up sport, even during brace treatment, because of its general health and psychological benefits. However, no sport straightens a curve on its own.
tur25-144: Scoliosis-specific exercises can help prevent progression of small curves and, in some patients, reduce the angle by a few degrees; but they are not expected to make the curve disappear completely. According to the 2024 Cochrane review of 13 studies, the certainty of the evidence on the benefits of exercise is low or very low. The treatment needed is decided by considering the curve angle and growth status together.
tur25-145: My curve is over 50 degrees; do I have to have surgery?
tur25-146: Not always. Surgery is usually recommended for young people who are still growing and whose curve is progressing beyond 45 degrees. In people who have finished growing, however, the decision is based not only on the angle but on whether the curve is progressing, trunk balance, pain, lung function and the person's expectations. In some patients whose trunk is balanced, whose curve is not progressing and whose daily life is not restricted, surgeons may recommend regular monitoring. You make the decision together with your spinal surgeon.
tur25-147: Does scoliosis progress after growth has finished?
tur25-148: Small curves usually do not progress. In a study in Denmark that followed patients treated with a brace or observation for 41 years on average, curves increased in adulthood by 0.2–0.5 degrees per year on average, but people differed widely. The authors recommend that people with moderate curves at the end of growth have one more X-ray check in early adulthood.
tur25-150: According to the SRS, pregnancy usually does not increase the curve in a spine that has not been operated on, and scoliosis does not make childbirth more difficult. Ask your obstetrician before starting exercise during pregnancy.
